title: On the applicability of Kolmogorov's theory of probability to the description of quantum phenomena. Part II: Bell inequalities
abstract: Among the various "no-go theorems" in the foundations of quantum mechanics, Bell inequalities are among the few, which do not implicitly rely on the mathematical structure of quantum mechanics. Instead, Bell inequalities are commonly understood to rest on Kolmogorov's theory of probability and a "locality" assumption. Physical evidence supporting their violation is hence taken as evidence against at least one of these two assumptions.   This work provides a comprehensive analysis of the physical debate on Bell inequalities from the point of view of Kolmogorov's theory of probability, focusing on the Bell-Clauser-Horn-Shimony-Holt inequality (BCHSH inequality). The central contribution is the motivation and mathematical study of the notion of contextuality in Bell experiments: in so-called contextual Bell models the detectors themselves behave randomly and the distribution of the random detector parameters depends on the chosen detector settings. It is shown how even "classical" Bell experiments motivate such a description. The need to account for contextuality was pointed out before by de la Peña, Cetto, Brody, Lochak, Bohm, Hiley and others. A broad class of contextual models is proven to satisfy the BCHSH inequality, thereby generalizing a previous result by Gill and Lambare. Nonetheless, even under strong locality requirements, contextual Bell models may violate the BCHSH inequality: based on work by Popescu and Rohrlich, we consider a "proof of concept" example exhibiting the maximum possible violation.   Contrary to the much debated "loopholes" in empirical tests of Bell inequalities, contextuality thus reveals a conceptual misunderstanding in the physical conclusions commonly drawn from Bell inequality violations.
summary: This paper re-examines Bell inequalities by analyzing them through the lens of Kolmogorov's probability theory, introducing the concept of contextuality. It demonstrates that even 'classical' models can be contextual, and crucially, that contextual models can violate Bell inequalities even under strong locality assumptions. This suggests that the physical conclusions drawn from Bell tests might stem from a conceptual misunderstanding regarding the nature of probability itself.
main_problem: The paper analyzes the applicability of Kolmogorov's theory of probability to quantum phenomena, specifically focusing on the implications of violating Bell inequalities.
main_result: Contextuality reveals a conceptual misunderstanding in the physical conclusions drawn from Bell inequality violations, suggesting that 'nonlocality' does not necessarily follow from empirical violations while respecting locality.
method: The analysis involves a comprehensive mathematical study of Bell experiments, focusing on the BCHSH inequality and introducing the notion of contextuality into the probabilistic framework.
model_or_system: The study uses the framework of Bell experiments, analyzing correlations between detector outcomes (A and B) for various settings (a, b), and comparing classical probabilistic models against quantum predictions.
key_observables: Expectation values, such as $\langle A(a), B(b) angle$, and the violation magnitude of the BCHSH inequality.
important_parameters: The settings of the detectors ($a, b$) and the underlying assumptions of locality and noncontextuality.
main_assumptions: The work critically examines the assumption of noncontextuality, which is a core assumption in the standard derivation of Bell inequalities.
paper_structure: The work is presented as Part II of a series, building upon foundational discussions of quantum mechanics and probability theory, and focusing specifically on the mathematical and physical interpretation of Bell inequalities.
why_interesting: It challenges the fundamental assumptions underlying the interpretation of quantum nonlocality, which is crucial for understanding measurement processes in quantum information and open quantum systems.
